title: Review: Periodic trends; Ionic bonding and lattices; Electronegativity, polarity and intermolecular forces
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT02#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD04#t1 term and clue written for the game; PT02#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD04#t3 term and clue written for the game. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Periodicity
items.clue: The pattern of trends repeating across each row of the table.

items.label: Electronegativity
items.clue: The ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair in a covalent bond.

items.label: Shielding
items.clue: Inner electrons repel outer ones, reducing the pull they feel from the nucleus.

items.label: London forces
items.clue: Electron movement makes a temporary dipole that induces one in a nearby molecule.

questions.stem: A student plans to measure the melting points of solid KF and solid KBr. Which prediction of the result, with its justification, is correct?

options.text: KBr will melt at the higher temperature, because KBr has the greater formula mass
KF will melt at the higher temperature, because F⁻ is smaller than Br⁻
KBr will melt at the higher temperature, because the larger Br⁻ attracts K⁺ more
Both will melt at about the same temperature, because the ion charges are equal

questions.explanation: Same charges, so size decides. F⁻ is smaller, the ion centres are closer and the attraction is stronger.

questions.stem: Diethyl ether, CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃, and 1-butanol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, are liquids with the same molecular formula, C₄H₁₀O. Which statement correctly compares their vapor pressures at 20 °C?

options.text: 1-Butanol's is higher, as its O–H groups form hydrogen bonds between molecules.
Diethyl ether's is higher, as its molecules cannot hydrogen bond with one another.
They are equal, as molecules of equal molar mass attract one another equally.
Diethyl ether's is higher, as its C–O bonds break far more easily than O–H bonds.

questions.explanation: Ether has no O–H. Dispersion forces are similar, so 1-butanol's hydrogen bonds decide.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energy of magnesium is lower than that of beryllium. Which explains this?

options.text: Magnesium has more electrons, so the nucleus's pull is shared among more of them.
Magnesium's outer electron is in shell 3, further from the nucleus and more shielded.
Magnesium's 3s electrons are paired, and their repulsion makes one easy to remove.
Magnesium is more reactive, so it gives up its outer electron more readily.

questions.explanation: Mg is [Ne] 3s², Be is 1s² 2s². The extra shell adds distance and shielding, which outweigh the larger nuclear charge (+12 against +4), so less energy is needed.

questions.stem: In a kettle's heating element, the hot metal wire is packed in powdered magnesium oxide, MgO, inside a metal tube. MgO is ionic, yet it is used here as an electrical insulator. Why doesn't it conduct?

options.text: MgO contains no ions until it is dissolved or melted.
Its ions are held in fixed positions, and MgO stays solid at the element's temperature.
Its electrons are all shared in covalent bonds, so none are free to move.
Its ions are too highly charged to move, even when MgO is molten.

questions.explanation: Charge flows only if charged particles can move. In the solid the ions are locked in the lattice and there are no free electrons. Strong 2+/2− attractions keep MgO solid to about 2850 °C.

questions.stem: The electronegativities of H, C and F are 2.20, 2.55 and 3.98, respectively. In a molecule of fluoromethane, CH₃F, the C atom is bonded to three H atoms and to the F atom. Which statement best describes the bonds in the molecule?

options.text: The C–H bonds and the C–F bond are equally polar, since each joins two different elements.
The C–H bonds are effectively nonpolar, and the C–F bond is ionic, with an F⁻ ion.
The C–H bonds and the C–F bond are nonpolar, since each is a pair of shared electrons.
The C–H bonds are effectively nonpolar, and the C–F bond is polar covalent, with F as δ−.

questions.stem: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine. Which explains this?

options.text: A fluorine atom has more protons than a chlorine atom, so it pulls harder on a shared pair.
Fluorine needs only one electron to fill its outer shell, so it attracts electrons strongly.
In fluorine the shared pair is closer to the nucleus and shielded by fewer inner electrons.
Fluorine releases more energy than chlorine when it gains an electron, so it is more electronegative.

questions.explanation: Fluorine's bonding electrons are in shell 2, shielded only by 1s². Chlorine's are in shell 3, shielded by 10 inner electrons. Shorter distance and less shielding outweigh chlorine's larger nuclear charge.

options.text: NH₄SO₄ for ammonium sulfate
NaCO₃ for sodium carbonate
Ca(OH)₂ for calcium hydroxide
AlNO₃ for aluminium nitrate

questions.explanation: One Ca²⁺ (2+) is balanced by two OH⁻ (2 × 1−). The bracket keeps each hydroxide ion whole.

questions.stem: A few crystals of I₂ are added to each of two test tubes, one containing water and the other containing hexane, C₆H₁₄, and both tubes are shaken. Which claim about the result, with its reasoning, is correct?

options.text: More I₂ dissolves in hexane, because I₂ and hexane molecules both interact through London dispersion forces.
More I₂ dissolves in hexane, because water molecules repel nonpolar I₂ molecules and push them out of the water.
More I₂ dissolves in water, because the strong attractions among water molecules make water the better solvent.
Equal amounts of I₂ dissolve in both, because shaking makes a solid dissolve in any liquid given enough time.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the energy released when a gaseous S atom gains an electron with the energy released when a gaseous Cl atom gains an electron, and explains the difference?

options.text: More is released for S, because Cl has more electrons, so its atom is larger and the added electron is farther away.
More is released for Cl, because gaining one electron gives a Cl atom a complete and stable octet.
The same amount is released for both, because the extra proton in Cl is cancelled out by the extra electron it has.
More is released for Cl, because the added electron enters the same shell but is attracted by one more proton.

questions.stem: A metal M in group 2 forms an ionic chloride that is 63.9% chlorine by mass. Based on the typical charges of the ions, what is the molar mass of M?

options.text: 10.0 g/mol
20.0 g/mol
40.1 g/mol
80.1 g/mol

questions.explanation: A group 2 metal forms M²⁺, so the chloride is MCl₂. The 70.90 g of Cl in one mole is 63.9% of the mass, so M is 70.90 × (36.1/63.9) = 40.1 g/mol.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃ (molar mass 17.0 g/mol), boils at −33 °C. Phosphine, PH₃ (34.0 g/mol), boils at −88 °C. Electronegativity: H 2.2, N 3.0, P 2.2. Why does the lighter molecule boil higher?

options.text: PH₃ molecules have no forces between them, because their P–H bonds are non-polar.
NH₃ has stronger London forces than PH₃, because it is the smaller molecule.
NH₃ molecules hydrogen bond to each other; PH₃ molecules cannot.
Boiling NH₃ breaks its N–H bonds, which are stronger than P–H bonds.

questions.explanation: N is very electronegative, so N–H is δ+ at H, and each N has a lone pair: N–H⋯N hydrogen bonds. P–H bonds are hardly polar (both 2.2), so PH₃ has no hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: An argon atom has seven more electrons than a sodium atom, yet argon's first ionisation energy is about three times sodium's. Which explains this?

options.text: Argon's outer shell is full, and a full shell is stable, so it does not want to lose an electron.
Argon has more electrons, so the extra electron–electron repulsion holds its outer electron in place.
Argon's outer electron is in a higher shell than sodium's, so it is held more tightly.
Argon has 18 protons to sodium's 11, and its outer electrons are in the same shell with similar shielding.
